# NYC Restroom Gap — plain-text edition for AI assistants

Generated from index.html of https://jonathanwong1990.github.io/nyc-restroom-gap/ (last updated 23 September 2026) by tools/build_llms.py.
Do not edit by hand. The web page embeds large SVG maps that are useless to a language
model; everything else from all three tabs is below. Read all three before answering
questions about reliability: the Walkthrough states findings, the Limits tab bounds them
and lists the open questions.

Hold onto three things. The ranking ORDERS neighbourhoods; it does not prove any single one
is underserved. No New York causal effect was measured (two designs failed, one on a
placebo set in advance), so there is no return-on-investment figure here. Items marked
[Team research: ...] come from teammates' research, checked against the primary source.

Authoritative sources, in order (the first outranks this file):
- https://github.com/JonathanWong1990/nyc-restroom-gap/blob/main/analysis/outputs/headline_numbers.json  (every number, with its script)
- https://github.com/JonathanWong1990/nyc-restroom-gap/blob/main/METHODS.md
- https://github.com/JonathanWong1990/nyc-restroom-gap

---

## Walkthrough

Items tagged [Team research] come from teammates' research, checked against the primary source before inclusion.

### 0 — The situation

- **Local Law 58** (May 2025) sets a target of **2,120** public restrooms by 2035. The City's register lists **975** operational today, so the gap is **1,145**.
- That is **11.5** restrooms per 100,000 residents today and **25.0** at the target.
- The City's siting strategy under the law is due on **1 Nov 2026**. [Team research: deadline reported by PIX11, Aug 2026]
- A **17-unit modular pilot** started in September 2026 ($4M, one year, open 7am–10pm). Its sites were published on 16 Sep: **none in Midtown**, and **4 in Astoria/Woodside**. [Team research: NYC Mayor's Office release, 16 Sep 2026]
- Earlier laws asked for sites but did not fund them: Local Law 114 of 2022 (find a feasible site in every ZIP code area) and Local Law 92 of 2025 (report on the projects at those sites). [Team research: Local Law 114 of 2022 and Local Law 92 of 2025 texts]

**The City has four decisions to make. We answer each one:** *where* to put restrooms, *when* they need to be open, *what to do first*, and *how to measure* the pilot it has already started.

### 1 — Where

Data cleaning, negative binomial regression, out-of-sample validation

**Our signal is 311 "Urinating in Public" complaints.** Nobody records "needed a toilet and could not find one", so this is the closest thing that is dated and mapped: 7,926 complaints from 2020 to 2026.

**Clean it first.** In East Harlem, **223 of 384** complaints came from five addresses on one block. Overall, the top 1% of addresses produce **22.3%** of complaints. We count each address once a month, which leaves **3,629**. Without this step, the ranking just follows whoever phones most often.

**Adjust for crowds.** Busy places generate more complaints, so for each of **197 neighbourhoods** the model predicts the number of complaints its subway riders, jobs, hotels and residents would normally produce. *Observed ÷ expected* is the **unmet-need ratio**. For example, Brighton Beach had 24 complaints against 6.2 expected, a ratio of 3.85×.

**Test it against a one-line rule.** The one-line rule ranks neighbourhoods by subway ridership alone. We fitted the model on 70% of neighbourhoods and scored it on the 30% it had not seen, repeated over 200 random splits. The model scores **0.788** against the rule's **0.703** (rank agreement with actual complaints) and wins in **96% of 200 splits**.

[Map: see the web page]

Shaded by observed ÷ expected complaints. Grey means the two match; darker means more complaints than the area's crowds explain.

**The answer: 29 neighbourhoods sit at 1.5× or more of their expected complaints.** Of these, six neighbourhoods clear 0.95 probability that true need is above 1.5×: East Harlem (North), Astoria (East)–Woodside (North), East Elmhurst, Williamsbridge–Olinville, Brighton Beach and Midtown–Times Square. The 1.5× cut-off is a budget line, not a natural boundary. Interactive map <https://jonathanwong1990.github.io/nyc-restroom-gap/maps/unmet-need.html>.

**Which corner within a neighbourhood?** A station-level screen of 424 subway complexes [Team research: station screen built on MTA ak4z-sape and NYC i7jb-7jku; reproduced from our data] measures the walk from each station to the nearest listed restroom. It works at a finer scale than our model and complements it. The two only partly agree, and that is expected: the screen ranks by ridership, which is the one-line rule our model beats. **Midtown–Times Square is the one place both flag independently.** The pilot has no unit there.

**Why the gap exists.** 824 of 1,066 listed restrooms are in parks, and capital money follows parkland rather than need. Midtown, with almost no parkland, has never had a Parks restroom project. Once crowds are accounted for, the number of restrooms in an area does not predict its complaints.

### 2 — When

Time-of-day coverage, hours parsing, station-level walking distance

**Complaints peak at 18:00**, and 30% are filed between 6pm and midnight. That is when restrooms close. Counting only restrooms with genuine posted hours, **24%** of the city's land is within a five-minute walk of an open restroom at 3pm, and **3.5%** at 9pm.

[Map: see the web page]

Covered at 3pm

Covered at 9pm

Share of each neighbourhood within a five-minute walk of a restroom open at that hour, counting only restrooms with genuine posted hours. Interactive map <https://jonathanwong1990.github.io/nyc-restroom-gap/maps/coverage-gap.html>.

The chart below combines two datasets. The team's station layer supplies the 50 busiest subway hubs, and our hours parser supplies which restrooms are open at each hour. It shows the walk from those hubs to the nearest restroom that is *open*. [Team research: station walk-distance layer (MTA ak4z-sape), combined with our parsed hours; script R/C2_hub_open_access.R]

[Chart: Line chart: entry-weighted walk from the 50 busiest subway hubs to the nearest open restroom, by hour of a typical weekday. About 3.7 minutes through the day, rising after 4pm and reaching 13.7 minutes at 9pm.] (img/hub_open_access.png)

Top 50 hubs, Wednesday, straight-line walk (real routes are longer, so these are lower bounds). Script: `R/C2_hub_open_access.R`.

| Top 50 hubs, Wednesday | Average walk | Hubs with no open restroom within 500 m |
|---|---|---|
| 2pm | 3.7 min | 4 of 50 |
| 6pm, off-season (park restrooms close 4pm) | 6.2 min | 21 of 50 |
| 6pm, in-season (park restrooms close 8pm) | 4.0 min | 9 of 50 |
| **9pm, either season** | **13.7 min** | **43 of 50** |

**Both seasons, stated honestly.** About two-thirds of listed restrooms show the same placeholder hours, "8am-4pm, Open later seasonally", so the true summer closing time is unknown. The 9pm result assumes park restrooms close by 9pm. If they stay open until 10pm, the 9pm figure improves to 5.9 min, with 20 of 50 hubs uncovered.

**"Open 24 hours" means a gas station.** The register lists 8 facilities as open 24 hours. All 8 are parkway gas stations or a parkway snack bar. [Team research: checked against NYC Open Data i7jb-7jku]

**Supply disappears when demand peaks.** Longer hours at existing restrooms, and the pilot's 10pm close, address the evening gap directly.

### 3 — What first

Panel data, facility fixed effects, placebo test, cost analysis

**The existing stock is deteriorating. This is our strongest result.** NYC Parks inspectors grade every comfort station on a schedule (31,768 inspections). The share rated unacceptable rose from **8.5%** in 2024 to **20.1%** in 2026, comparing the same January–June window each year.

- **It is the same buildings getting worse.** With facility fixed effects, 2026 is +11.4 pp above 2024.
- **It is not stricter inspectors.** The 7 inspectors who rated restrooms in both years marked litter slightly *better* (0.016 → 0.011) while structural failures rose from 0.044 to 0.210. Only the building fabric got worse.
- **An independent audit agrees.** The City Council's "Good to Go?" audit (Aug–Sep 2025, random sample) found **36 of 337** rooms closed during posted hours, all of them in parks, and **129 of 301** open rooms missing a basic necessity. [Team research: NYC Council Oversight & Investigations, 'Good to Go?' report, Dec 2025]
- 80 of 736 Parks comfort stations are under long-term closure, 46 of them for repairs.

| Option | Cost | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Build a new restroom | **$4.0M** | Median of 68 NYC capital projects. DDC's 2026 contract works out at $3.86M per building [Team research: NYC DDC press release, 26 Jun 2026] |
| Reconstruct an existing one | **$1.66M** | Median of 108 projects |
| Modular unit (Portland Loo) | **$1.2M** | NYC Parks' $6M pilot for five Portland Loos |
| Extend hours: 51 restrooms in 10 areas, 4 more hours a day | **$2.6M a year** | Assumes $35/h staffing; $26.1M over ten years ($22.2M present value at 3%) |

**Extending hours is not free.** Taking the cheapest fix that each of the 29 places allows (9 build, 8 reconstruct, 10 extend hours, 2 monitor) costs **$24.1M in capital**, and the extra hours add up to **$2.6M a year** in running cost on top.

**Cheapest per excess complaint.** Measured by annual cost per excess complaint, the cheapest single action is longer hours in East Harlem (North), at $775 a year. Reconstructions no longer top the list; the first is 7th. Two caveats:

- The comparison prices longer hours as one extra attendant per area ($51,100 a year). If every restroom needs its own staffing, modular units in Astoria (East)–Woodside (North) become cheapest, and East Harlem falls to 9th.
- Hours stay cheapest only while staffing costs less than about $100/h. An earlier version said the ranking did not depend on the wage. That was wrong.

**Fix before you build.** The case does not rest on cost per complaint. It rests on three things: the stock is measurably decaying, a reconstruction costs well under half as much as a new build, and a typical restroom capital project takes a median 5.2 years from design to completion. A closed restroom serves nobody, while a reopened one serves whoever is there.

### 4 — How to measure the pilot

Stage gates, cost-effectiveness metric, randomised staggered trial, power analysis

**Judge the pilot on hours it is actually open, not on the number of units installed.** [Team research: stage-gate and cost-per-verified-open-hour framing, rewritten; DC pilot statute (D.C. Act 25-172) for monthly reporting]

- **Cost per verified open hour.** Divide total cost by the hours each unit was actually found open and working, not by the hours it was scheduled. Measured against scheduled hours, the pilot costs **$42.98** per unit-hour ($4M ÷ 17 units × 15 hours × 365 days). Any closure pushes the true figure up.
- **Stage gates.** Verify that a site is really underserved, confirm the unit is open and working, then scale up. Only after that should a site get a permanent building.
- **Data to require from the operator**, site by site and week by week: open and closed timestamps, uses, faults, time to repair, and cost. Washington DC's pilot law requires monthly reports on use by date and time and on misuse.

**Our trial design, for the hours option.** Extend hours in the 10 areas in a random, staggered order over ten months, with each area compared against its own history. Complaints are too sparse to detect anything short of a 156% change. Public-urination summonses can detect a **37%** change. **Caveat:** summonses track policing. We rejected them for *ranking* places for exactly that reason, and extra opening hours could themselves change patrols. Alcohol summonses serve as the placebo.

**What other cities show.** In San Francisco, 13 new Pit Stop restrooms were followed by −12.47 feces reports a week (p = 0.0002; Amato et al., *BMC Public Health*, 2022). A 2025 follow-up covering 2009–2022 found that "the effect appears to be small". [Team research: PLOS ONE, 14 Aug 2025 ('Privy by the Bay')] Neither study is from NYC, so treat them as evidence that an effect is possible, not as a forecast for New York.

What other cities do [Team research: peer-city operating models; each link opened 23 Sep 2026]

- San Francisco Pit Stop <https://sfpublicworks.org/pitstop>: every restroom has a paid attendant; the study above evaluated it.
- Washington DC pilot <https://dcpublicrestrooms.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/Public-Restroom-Pilot-Program.pdf>: the law requires monthly data on use and misuse.
- Paris <https://opendata.paris.fr/explore/dataset/sanisettesparis/>: every public toilet is in one open dataset, with its hours and accessibility.
- Tokyo Toilet <https://tokyotoilet.jp/en/maintenance/>: a fixed daily, monthly and annual cleaning schedule, checked by outside inspectors.
- City of London <https://www.cityoflondon.gov.uk/services/streets/clean-streets/public-toilets>: pays businesses to let the public use their toilets.
- Portland Loo in NYC <https://www.nyc.gov/mayors-office/news/2025/07/mayor-adams-nyc-parks-commissioner-rodriguez-rosa-continue-we-outside-summer-announcing>: NYC Parks' $6M pilot for five units.

### 5 — What we recommend

| Who | Do this |
|---|---|
| Mayor's Office (LL58 strategy, due 1 Nov) | Site new units using the need ranking, not raw complaints or ridership. Start with the six high-confidence areas, and name Midtown–Times Square explicitly |
| NYC Parks | Reconstruct and reopen closed comfort stations before building new ones, and publish real closing times in place of the placeholder |
| DOT (plazas and sidewalks) | Put modular units on streets where parks cannot reach, starting in Midtown, and require site-week open-hour data |
| MTA | Use the hub-by-hour screen to decide which busy stations need an open restroom nearby after 6pm |

### 6 — How we know it holds up

- The model scores 0.784–0.791 across six random seeds. A decision tree scores 0.720.
- Adding 1,886 chain cafés and fast-food outlets as informal supply leaves the ranking unchanged (0.997).
- Each of the six high-confidence areas was re-scored with itself left out, and all held.
- **The weak points:** the ranking does not fully survive a phone-only check; the ratio may partly track street homelessness or nightlife; and our two attempts to prove causally that toilets reduce the problem failed. All of these are in the Limits tab, alongside the open questions.

---

## Limits and open questions

This tab collects every weakness in one place, starting with the questions we have not yet answered.

### Open questions: not yet resolved

These are the three hardest objections to our analysis. None has a full answer yet.

1. **The need ratio may partly map street homelessness or nightlife.** The model adjusts for subway riders, jobs, hotels and residents. It has no control for shelters, unsheltered counts, bars or late-night licences. A neighbourhood with many people living on the street, or a busy bar strip, could show a high ratio for reasons a new restroom would only partly fix. We have not yet tested this.
2. **The confidence figures and the phone-only check point in different directions.** East Harlem (North) and Astoria (East)–Woodside (North) both have a posterior probability above 0.999. Yet if we re-rank using only complaints filed by phone, East Harlem falls to 41st and Astoria to 121st, and Williamsbridge–Olinville falls to 50th. The two results fit together once you see what the posterior assumes: it measures how sure we are *given that complaints measure need*. The phone-only check questions that assumption. The right reading is "very sure there are excess *complaints* here", which is weaker than "very sure there is excess *need*". Of the high-confidence areas checked, Brighton Beach and East Elmhurst hold under both.
3. **The trial outcome is the one we rejected for ranking.** Across neighbourhoods, urination summonses correlate 0.95 with alcohol summonses, which means they map policing more than need. We therefore did not use them to rank places. In a before-and-after design each area is compared with itself, so constant enforcement cancels out. But if opening restrooms for longer changes patrol patterns, it does not cancel. The alcohol-summons placebo would catch a general shift in patrolling, though not one aimed specifically at restroom areas.

### 1. The ranking orders places; it does not sort them into categories

Complaint counts are thin, so there are two things to check.

- **Is the variation real?** Yes. The spread across neighbourhoods is wider than chance alone would produce.
- **Are the worst places a separate group?** No. Suppose every neighbourhood genuinely differed by exactly the spread we estimated. Simulations of that city throw up 33.8 neighbourhoods above 1.5× on average; we found 29. Need shades continuously from the top of the list downwards, so the 1.5× threshold is a budget decision, not a discovery.
- **How sure are we about one place?** The posterior probabilities (Walkthrough, "Where") answer this. Six neighbourhoods clear 0.95; East Flatbush–Rugby just misses at 0.948. Each result held when the neighbourhood was left out of the model and the prior. A formal correction for testing all 197 places at once would clear none of them. So the honest claim is about where to look and where to spend first, not a proven fact about any single place.

### 2. We never validated the thing we actually deliver

The model predicts complaints well: 0.788 against the one-line rule's 0.703, scored on neighbourhoods it had not seen. But what we deliver is the *gap* between prediction and reality, and nothing can validate that gap, because "true unmet need" has never been measured. The better the model predicts, the less gap is left to rank. Excess-mortality estimates work the same way, but they rest on counts in the thousands; ours are in the tens.

### 3. We cannot yet show that a restroom reduces street urination in New York

We tried two causal designs. Both failed:

- **Closures.** The inspection records flagged as "closures" turned out mostly to log construction activity, not real closures, so there was nothing to measure.
- **Winter closures.** Seasonal restrooms shut every winter while year-round ones stay open, which looks like a natural experiment. Urination summonses near seasonal sites fell (IRR 0.624). But the placebo, alcohol summonses, fell almost as much (IRR 0.699). Parks empty out in winter, so we had measured the season, not the restroom.

So this project contains no New York effect estimate, and no return-on-investment figure. Published evidence does exist from elsewhere. In San Francisco, Amato et al. (*BMC Public Health*, 2022) found −12.47 feces reports a week after 13 new Pit Stop restrooms opened. A 2025 follow-up in *PLOS ONE* found "the effect appears to be small". What does not exist is a US cost-benefit study. Our break-even figures show how large an effect would have to be to justify the spend; they are not a measured effect.

### 4. The cost comparison depends on assumptions

- The $24.1M capital figure counts extending hours as zero *capital*. Its running cost is $2.6M a year for 51 restrooms, which is $26.1M over ten years undiscounted.
- The staffing cost ($35/h) and the extra hours per day (4) are assumptions, not sourced figures. Extending hours stops being the cheapest option at about $100/h.
- The cost-per-complaint ranking prices extending hours as one attendant per area ($51,100 a year). If each restroom needs its own staffing, East Harlem (North) falls from 1st to 9th.
- Installing a unit in all 29 places would cost $34.8M (29 × the $1.2M Parks pilot price). Of course the cheapest-fix mix costs less than that; the comparison is true by construction and is not a finding.
- The modular price ($1.2M, from NYC Parks' Portland Loo pilot) is for a unit connected to water and sewer. The 2026 pilot's $235k per unit-year is a service contract (units plus cleaning), so the two figures are not comparable.

### 5. Complaints measure complainers

- Neighbourhood complaint counts correlate 0.31 with the share of reports filed online.
- On phone-only reports, three of the six high-confidence areas drop sharply (see the open questions above).
- The person who complains and the person who needed a toilet are different people. To some extent we are measuring annoyance.
- We tested police summonses as an alternative: they are 27,384 records and far denser. They correlate 0.95 with alcohol summonses, so they map enforcement. We kept complaints.

### 6. The parks explanation is inferred, not measured

Three facts point the same way. 824 of 1,066 restrooms are in parks. Once crowds are accounted for, supply shows no link with complaints. Capital money follows parkland. But we never compared park-sited with street-sited restrooms directly, because there are too few street-sited ones to compare.

### 7. The trial is blunt

Measured on 311 complaints, the trial could only detect a change of 156%, or 433% using phone-filed reports alone. Measured on summonses, it can detect 37%. That is enough to catch a large effect but not a modest one, and the summons outcome carries the policing caveat in open question 3.

### 8. The deterioration finding is strong, but not airtight

- **The within-inspector test rests on 7 people.** Standard errors clustered on seven inspectors are unreliable.
- **A gradual shift in inspector emphasis cannot be ruled out.** A rule change would show up as a step; the data shows a steady climb. New inspectors fail restrooms less often, not more. We found no published change to the inspection method, but that does not prove there was none.
- **Park-wide condition makes a poor placebo.** Parks without a comfort station improved while parks with one got worse, so the citywide average hides two opposite movements. Site condition also moves with restroom condition. We rely instead on the internal placebo: the same inspector on the same visit marked litter as flat while structural failures rose.
- **2026 is a part year.** Every year is compared on the same January–June window.
- **It measures condition, not siting.** The siting question still rests on complaints.
- **Component-repair costs are too thin to quote.** Only 5 projects in the capital tracker are component work.

### 9. Data problems worth knowing

- **Placeholder hours.** 525 of the 843 year-round restrooms have the same text: "8am-4pm, Open later seasonally". The City's own register cannot say what is open at 9pm.
- **A stale register.** Its rows were last updated on 27 June 2025. The City Council's dashboard says 973 are operational; the register gives 975, and we use the register. The dashboard's "49.42% within a five-minute walk" has no published method, so we do not use it.
- **The capital tracker repeats rows.** Its entries cover 191 restroom projects, and bundled entries repeat costs. Many projects give only a cost band, and those are the expensive ones, which is why the pooled median is $2,331,000.
- **Retired 311 complaint types** return zero rows without any warning.

### 10. Datasets that looked useful and were not

| Dataset | Why we dropped it |
|---|---|
| Police summonses | Map enforcement, not need (0.95 with alcohol summonses) |
| Cultural organisations | A grants roster: a small theatre collective and the Met each count as one row |
| Pedestrian counts | Only 114 counting points for the whole city |
| Chain cafés and fast-food outlets (1,886) | No effect on the ranking (0.997 agreement) |
| A hand-weighted station index | Built from ridership and distance, never checked against an outcome, and its top-20 list changes with the weights. That is why we modelled complaints |

Every dataset and script is listed in the **Data & code** tab.

---

## Data and code

Everything behind this analysis is public and can be run: 49 R scripts, every dataset exactly as pulled, and the models that failed alongside the ones that worked.

### Run it yourself

```
git clone https://github.com/JonathanWong1990/nyc-restroom-gap
cd nyc-restroom-gap/analysis
Rscript R/11_benchmark.R
Rscript R/Z0_headline_numbers.R   # rebuilds every number quoted on this site
```

You need R 4.6.1 and these packages: `sf`, `dplyr`, `MASS`, `tidyr`, `data.table`, `sandwich`, `lmtest`, `rpart`, `leaflet`, `htmlwidgets`, `httr`, `jsonlite`. The scripts read `data_raw/` relative to the working directory; to run them from anywhere else, set `RESTROOM_PROJ` to the `analysis/` folder. You do not need API keys or any downloads.

### Where the numbers come from

Every figure on this site is taken from `analysis/outputs/headline_numbers.json` <https://github.com/JonathanWong1990/nyc-restroom-gap/blob/main/analysis/outputs/headline_numbers.json>. `R/Z0_headline_numbers.R` writes that file by reading the raw data or running the script that owns each number. `R/Z1_check_site.R` then checks that this page, llms.txt <https://jonathanwong1990.github.io/nyc-restroom-gap/llms.txt> and the README quote those values and none of the known-wrong ones. Outside facts (laws, press releases, studies) sit in the file's `external` block, each with its URL.

### If you are handing this to an AI

1. **`llms.txt` <https://jonathanwong1990.github.io/nyc-restroom-gap/llms.txt>**: this page as plain text, generated from this HTML.
2. **`analysis/outputs/headline_numbers.json`**: every number, with the script it came from.
3. **`METHODS.md`**: what each script does.
4. **`analysis/notes/`**: one file per workstream, with external citations and access dates.

| `A1_noise_floor.R` <https://github.com/JonathanWong1990/nyc-restroom-gap/blob/main/analysis/R/A1_noise_floor.R>, `A3_seed_stability.R` <https://github.com/JonathanWong1990/nyc-restroom-gap/blob/main/analysis/R/A3_seed_stability.R>, `96_commercial_supply.R` <https://github.com/JonathanWong1990/nyc-restroom-gap/blob/main/analysis/R/96_commercial_supply.R>, `A4_reporting_channel.R` <https://github.com/JonathanWong1990/nyc-restroom-gap/blob/main/analysis/R/A4_reporting_channel.R> | Robustness checks |
| `93_winterization.R` <https://github.com/JonathanWong1990/nyc-restroom-gap/blob/main/analysis/R/93_winterization.R>, `12–15_did_*.R`, `90–92_*.R` | **Failed, kept on purpose:** two causal designs and the rejected summons outcome |
| `Z0_headline_numbers.R` <https://github.com/JonathanWong1990/nyc-restroom-gap/blob/main/analysis/R/Z0_headline_numbers.R>, `Z1_check_site.R` <https://github.com/JonathanWong1990/nyc-restroom-gap/blob/main/analysis/R/Z1_check_site.R> | The numbers file and the site checker |

The full script-by-script list is in METHODS.md <https://github.com/JonathanWong1990/nyc-restroom-gap/blob/main/METHODS.md>. `demand_02_hourprofile.R` is orphaned: do not run it.

### Every dataset we used

All datasets were pulled on 20 September 2026. Row counts are what came out of the source; the figures used in the analysis are lower after cleaning.

| Dataset | ID | Rows | Used for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Public restrooms | `i7jb-7jku` <https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/i7jb-7jku> | 1,066 | Supply: location, type, hours |
| 311 urination / public toilet | `erm2-nwe9` <https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/erm2-nwe9> | 8,193 | **The outcome** |
| 311 dirty conditions | `erm2-nwe9` <https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/erm2-nwe9> | 108,775 | Control for the report-time test |
| OATH summonses: urination | `hxbk-grd3` <https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/hxbk-grd3> | 27,384 | Rejected for ranking; the trial's outcome |
| OATH summonses: alcohol | `hxbk-grd3` <https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/hxbk-grd3> | 163,329 | The placebo |
| ACS 5-year 2024, tracts | US Census | 2,327 | Residents, income, age |
| LEHD LODES8 WAC 2023 | US Census | 25,445 | Workers |
| Taxi and for-hire trips by zone-month | `c5iv-bn4s` <https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/c5iv-bn4s> | 138,706 | Floating demand |
| Subway ridership, monthly | `ak4z-sape` <https://data.ny.gov/d/ak4z-sape> | 48,255 | Transit exposure; hub ranking |
| Subway stations | `39hk-dx4f` <https://data.ny.gov/d/39hk-dx4f> | 496 | Station locations |
| Hotels | `tjus-cn27` <https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/tjus-cn27> | 14,010 | Visitors |
| Parks properties | `enfh-gkve` <https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/enfh-gkve> | 2,061 | Parkland |
| Parks capital tracker | `4hcv-tc5r` <https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/4hcv-tc5r> | 2,787 | Build and reconstruct costs; delivery time |
| PIP inspections (master) | `yg3y-7juh` <https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/yg3y-7juh> | 152,484 | Condition trend |
| PIP restrooms (closure flags) | `9byw-znpj` <https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/9byw-znpj> | 736 | Long-term closures |
| PIP all sites | `buk3-3qpr` <https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/buk3-3qpr> | 6,406 | Inspection site register |
| Park structures | `n8q6-i44s` <https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/n8q6-i44s> | 2,857 | Cross-check on the inventory |
| Comfort-station COVID closures | `i5n2-q8ck` <https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/i5n2-q8ck> | 672 | Closure history (not a usable experiment) |
| Taxi zones | `8meu-9t5y` <https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/8meu-9t5y> | 263 | Joining taxi trips to geography |
| NTA 2020 · tracts 2020 · community districts | `9nt8-h7nd` <https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/9nt8-h7nd> · `63ge-mke6` <https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/63ge-mke6> · `5crt-au7u` <https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/5crt-au7u> | — | Units of analysis and clustering |
| Cultural organisations (not used) | `u35m-9t32` <https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/u35m-9t32> | 2,535 | See Limits §10 |
| Pedestrian counts (not used) | `cqsj-cfgu` <https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/cqsj-cfgu> | 114 | See Limits §10 |
| Chain food outlets (robustness only) | `43nn-pn8j` <https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/43nn-pn8j> | 1,886 | See Limits §10 |

Files are in `analysis/data_raw/`, named `<source>_<id>_<date>.csv`. The outcome is 311 public-urination complaints from 2020 to September 2026, de-duplicated to one per address per month: 3,629 citywide, of which 3,556 fall inside the 197 residential neighbourhoods we model.

### Merged from team research

Each item below is tagged [Team research] where it appears. Every one was checked against its primary source before inclusion.

| Item | Where | Primary source |
|---|---|---|
| LL58 strategy due 1 Nov 2026 | Situation | PIX11, Aug 2026 <https://pix11.com/news/local-news/deadline-delayed-for-plan-to-expand-nyc-public-bathrooms/> |
| 17-unit pilot and its sites | Situation | NYC Mayor's Office, Sep 2026 <https://www.nyc.gov/mayors-office/news/2026/09/mayor-mamdani-brings-17-new-public-bathrooms-to-neighborhoods-ac> |
| Local Laws 114 (2022) and 92 (2025) | Situation | LL114 text <https://intro.nyc/local-laws/2022-114> · Council on LL92 <https://council.nyc.gov/press/2025/07/12/2922/> |
| Station-level screen | Where | MTA `ak4z-sape` <https://data.ny.gov/d/ak4z-sape> + NYC `i7jb-7jku` <https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/i7jb-7jku> (reproduced from our data) |
| Hub × hours chart | When | Same station layer combined with our parsed hours; `R/C2_hub_open_access.R` |
| The 8 "24-hour" facilities are parkway gas stations or a parkway snack bar | When | NYC `i7jb-7jku` <https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/i7jb-7jku> |
| Council "Good to Go?" audit | What first | NYC Council OID report, Dec 2025 <https://council.nyc.gov/press/wp-content/uploads/sites/56/2025/12/OID_Restrooms-REPORT_121625-v4.pdf> |
| DDC $3.86M per building | What first | NYC DDC, 26 Jun 2026 <https://www.nyc.gov/site/ddc/about/press-releases/2026/pr-062626-MurphyBros.page> |
| Cost per verified open hour; stage gates; operator data spec | How to measure | Framing rewritten in our words; DC reporting rule: D.C. Act 25-172 <https://dcpublicrestrooms.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/Public-Restroom-Pilot-Program.pdf> |
| 2025 San Francisco follow-up study | How to measure | PLOS ONE, Aug 2025 <https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0327795> |
| Peer-city box | How to measure | Links in the box, each opened 23 Sep 2026 |

We did not take four things from the team's research: a per-capita "well-served" range we could not trace to any source; a 24-hour comparison with Paris built on mismatched denominators; a phase-one budget envelope that no analysis produced; and hand-weighted station indices.
